newsitem.title: FRANCE: Alcatel to launch network satellite in 2001.
newsitem.headline: Alcatel to launch network satellite in 2001.

text.p: Alcatel Espace, a division of Alcatel Alsthom, said on Wednesday it will launch the first satellite in its 64-satellite Skybridge global telecoms network in 2001.

Jean-Claude Husson, chairman and chief executive of Alcatel Espace, told a news briefing in Toulouse, southern France, that he was aiming at a 25 percent share of the satellite telecoms market estimated at more than $30 billion by 2010.

He predicted that rival satellite communications projects such as the Teledesic project of Microsoft chief executive Bill Gates and cellular phone mogul Craig McCaw, would not be ready at the start of the next millennium due to industrial constraints and limited launch possibilities.

Herve Sorre, marketing executive for Skybridge, said that Skybridge would cost some private users $40 per month, on top of a $700 investment in a satellite dish, and between $100 and $150 per month for professional users.

"We believe that Skybridge could have between 15 and 20 million users at the end of the first generation of satellites, that is to say in 2010. We should have a market share of about 25 percent," he said.

While Teledesic hopes to launch 840 satellites, Skybridge is limited to 64 satellites. Husson said the first investment partners in the $3.5 billion Skybridge project would join by the end of June and would include U.S. satellite maker Loral.
Husson said that France Telecom was also considering joining the project.
He said he would prefer strategic alliances with firms like Dasa of Daimler-Benz, Aerospatiale and Alenia before proposing a deal to Matra.
Matra is part of the Lagardere Groupe, Alcatel's rival in the bidding for the state's 58 percent stake in defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF.
"If the privatisation of Thomson-CSF goes in our favour, that will strengthen us strategically," Husson said.
But even without Thomson-CSF, the Alcatel unit expects a sales growth of 20 percent per year between now and 2000, compared to 2.87 billion francs in 1996.

Alcatel filed for a U.S. Federal Communications Commission licence in February for the Skybridge project, which is intended to provide high-capacity Internet access as well as other applications like teleworking, education at a distance and mobile telecommunications.
Sorre said four to five rocket launches would suffice to put the 64 satellites, each weighing some 800 kgs, into orbit.
He expected Europe and the U.S. would represent one-third each of the market with Asia accounting for 25 percent.
He added that Alcatel would not compete with local telecoms operators but would instead provide services to them.
